drafts.topic: Social proof: why people trust what other people are already doing

post.hook: Why do we follow the crowd?
slides: We look to others when unsure which product fits us.
Study: 2007 shoppers preferred items **most others** purchased.
Our brain treats group choices as a shortcut to safety.
Brands add **customer testimonials**, **review counts**, or “trending now” badges to boost trust.
When a product shows **5-star rating**, conversion rates often jump noticeably.
post.takeaway: Show real social proof, reviews, ratings, user counts, to guide prospects toward buying.
post.caption:
Ever wonder why a product with dozens of reviews feels safer than an unknown one? It's not magic, it's psychology.

When we’re uncertain, we lean on the choices of others. Studies show people pick items that **most others** buy, using the crowd as a shortcut to safety.

Brands tap this by displaying **customer testimonials**, **review counts**, or “trending now” tags. Even a simple **5-star rating** can lift conversion rates.

What social proof element has worked best for your business?

drafts.topic: "$365 a year" vs "$1 a day": reframing a price into a smaller unit

post.hook: Are you pricing in the wrong unit?
slides: Why it falls flat: big number feels costly, triggers loss aversion.
Principle: **Unit Bias**, people prefer smaller, familiar units.
Why it works: daily unit feels trivial, lowers perceived cost.
post.takeaway: Break large prices into small, familiar units to make offers feel affordable instantly.
post.caption:
Ever wondered why a $365 yearly fee feels pricey, while $1 a day sounds almost free? It’s not magic, it’s **Unit Bias** at work. When we see a smaller, familiar unit, our brain treats the cost as negligible.

By simply reframing the same price into daily or weekly amounts, you lower the perceived barrier and boost conversion. Try swapping "$299 per month" for "just $10 a day" in your next email or landing page.

What other price formats have you tested? Share your results below!
